subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: 'Labelling' in education refers to teachers:
options: Streaming pupils by exam results only
Attaching meanings or definitions (e.g. 'bright' or 'troublemaker') to pupils
questions.explain: Labelling is when teachers define pupils in particular ways, which can shape how they are treated and perform.

questions.q: A common explanation for boys' relative underachievement is the idea of a 'crisis of masculinity', linked to:
options: The decline of traditional manual jobs reducing male motivation
questions.explain: The decline of traditional male manual work is argued to undermine some boys' motivation and identity, affecting achievement.

questions.q: In studies of ethnicity and achievement, the concept of 'institutional racism' refers to:
options: The ethnocentric national curriculum being abolished
Routine, often unintended discrimination built into the normal workings of an institution
questions.explain: Institutional racism describes discrimination embedded in an institution's everyday practices and structures, not just individuals.

questions.q: Althusser argued that education is part of the:
questions.explain: Althusser saw education as an ideological state apparatus reproducing class inequality and transmitting ruling-class ideology.

questions.q: Academies and free schools, expanded under the Coalition from 2010, are characterised by:
options: The return of the 11-plus for all
Greater independence from local authority control
questions.explain: Academies and free schools have greater autonomy from local authorities, reflecting continued marketisation.

questions.q: The 1988 Education Reform Act is most associated with which key change?
options: Introducing marketisation, league tables, formula funding and open enrolment
questions.explain: The 1988 Act introduced marketisation: a national curriculum, league tables, open enrolment and competition between schools.

questions.q: 'Streaming' is best defined as:
options: Placing pupils into classes of similar overall ability for all subjects
questions.explain: Streaming groups pupils by general ability across subjects, and is linked to labelling and subculture formation.

questions.q: Compensatory education programmes (e.g. Sure Start) are based on which theory of underachievement?
questions.explain: Compensatory schemes assume cultural deprivation and try to make up for supposed deficiencies in the home.

questions.q: Tony Sewell's explanation for some Black Caribbean boys' underachievement emphasised:
options: The influence of anti-school street/peer subcultures and lack of positive role models
questions.explain: Sewell pointed to peer-group pressure and anti-school 'street' subcultures, plus absent role models, while rejecting purely racist explanations.

questions.q: The New Right view of education most strongly favours which of the following?
options: Marketisation, competition and parental choice to raise standards
A national curriculum imposed with no parental choice
questions.explain: The New Right favours marketisation and competition, believing choice and competition between schools raise standards.

questions.q: The 'hidden curriculum' refers to:
options: The values, norms and attitudes transmitted implicitly through school routines
Subjects taught only in private schools
questions.explain: The hidden curriculum is the set of unofficial lessons (e.g. obedience, punctuality) learned through school organisation.

questions.q: Which New Labour policy aimed to tackle deprivation by targeting funding at disadvantaged areas and pupils?
options: Education Action Zones / Education Maintenance Allowance (EMA)
questions.explain: New Labour introduced measures like EAZs and EMA to reduce inequality, alongside marketisation policies.

questions.q: The concept of 'parentocracy', associated with marketisation, refers to:
options: Rule of the education system by teachers
The idea that parents have power and choice over their children's schooling
questions.explain: Parentocracy ('rule by parents') describes the marketised system in which parents exercise choice between schools.

questions.q: The 1944 Education Act introduced which system, dividing pupils via the 11-plus exam?
questions.explain: The 1944 Act created the tripartite system (grammar, secondary modern, technical), selecting pupils by the 11-plus.

questions.q: Lacey's concepts of 'differentiation' and 'polarisation' help explain the formation of:
questions.explain: Lacey argued streaming (differentiation) polarises pupils into pro-school and anti-school subcultures.

questions.q: Bowles and Gintis argued that the structure of school mirrors the workplace through which principle?
questions.explain: The correspondence principle states that the social relationships of school correspond to those of the capitalist workplace.

questions.q: Which sociologist saw education as creating 'social solidarity' and transmitting society's shared norms and values?
questions.explain: Durkheim argued education transmits shared culture, creating social solidarity and a sense of belonging.

questions.q: Bernstein distinguished between two language patterns; which 'code' is said to advantage middle-class pupils in school?
questions.explain: Bernstein argued the elaborated code used by the middle class matches that of schools, giving them an advantage.

questions.q: Parsons described the school as a 'bridge' between the family and wider society because it operates on which principle?
questions.explain: Parsons argued school applies universalistic, meritocratic standards, bridging the particularistic family and society.

questions.q: The functionalist claim that education is meritocratic is most directly challenged by which evidence?
options: The persistence of social class differences in attainment
The introduction of the national curriculum
questions.explain: Persistent class (and other) gaps in achievement challenge the functionalist claim that education rewards pure ability.

questions.q: The 'self-fulfilling prophecy' in education describes a process where:
options: A label or prediction becomes true because of how pupils are then treated
Pupils choose their own subjects freely
questions.explain: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when a label leads to treatment that makes the prediction come true (e.g. Rosenthal and Jacobson).

questions.q: Davis and Moore's functionalist theory of education is best summarised as:
options: Education is an ideological state apparatus
Education sifts and sorts people into roles via 'role allocation' and is meritocratic
questions.explain: Davis and Moore argue education sifts and sorts individuals into appropriate roles, justifying unequal rewards by ability.

questions.q: Which concept describes the lack of attitudes, values and skills needed for educational success, said to be passed on in the home?
questions.explain: Cultural deprivation theory argues some working-class children lack the cultural equipment (values, language, knowledge) for success.

questions.q: Rosenthal and Jacobson's 'Pygmalion in the Classroom' study is most associated with demonstrating:
questions.explain: Their study suggested teacher expectations of 'spurters' produced real gains, illustrating the self-fulfilling prophecy.

questions.q: Keddie criticised cultural deprivation theory by arguing that working-class children are:
options: Not deprived but culturally different, and wrongly judged by middle-class standards
questions.explain: Keddie argued children cannot be 'deprived of their own culture'; they are culturally different and unfairly judged by school norms.

questions.q: 'Material deprivation' as an explanation for working-class underachievement refers to:
options: A lack of the right attitudes and values at home
A lack of money and the resources it buys (housing, books, diet)
questions.explain: Material deprivation is the lack of physical/economic resources such as adequate housing, diet and study space.

questions.q: Durkheim argued that, by teaching subjects like maths, schools also provide pupils with which essential skill for industrial society?
options: Specialist skills needed for a complex division of labour
questions.explain: Durkheim argued education teaches the specialist skills required by an advanced division of labour.

questions.q: For Bowles and Gintis, the 'myth of meritocracy' functions to:
options: Legitimise and disguise class inequality by blaming individuals for failure
questions.explain: Bowles and Gintis argue meritocracy is a myth that justifies inequality and persuades people failure is their own fault.

questions.q: Feminists argue the education system has historically reinforced gender inequality through:
options: A gendered hidden curriculum and subject 'channelling'
questions.explain: Feminists point to gendered subject choices, textbooks and the hidden curriculum that channel girls and boys differently.

questions.q: Paul Willis's study 'Learning to Labour' found that the working-class 'lads':
options: Formed an anti-school subculture yet ended up in working-class jobs
questions.explain: Willis found the 'lads' resisted school through a counter-culture but ironically prepared themselves for low-skilled labour.
